steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Spacerini, a tool for building and sharing search engines over text datasets with Pyserini and Hugging Face. Motivate it with the problem of auditing huge training datasets, mention who else could use it, and say what the tool does.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Data commoditization and datasets too big to document
- Consequences: models trained on poorly understood data, harms; need to audit training data
- Spacerini's origin and wider audience
- What Spacerini does and how

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The commoditization of data has transformed data-driven computer science in general, and machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) in particular. The race to train larger and larger language models depends so much on having access to huge amounts of text that the datasets have become "too big to document", as one paper claims, both technically and methodologically. In practice this often leads to training first and asking questions later, which is an example of a convenience experiment, meaning a research approach that depends on the availability of a resource and on how easy a method is rather than on whether it suits the problem. In this sense, some authors believe it is important to distinguish between the availability of data and its appropriateness, especially because of the misconception that web data represents all human experience and is immune to the digital divide, which keeps getting wider. They suggest that the divide exists and also limits the representativeness of the web, and this in turn reinforces the biases of the artifacts that use it.

Since large datasets can't be easily audited, researchers are incentivized to release models trained on data they don't really understand, and this leads to model behaviors that are hard to study, predict or trace. This is especially a problem because of the real-world harms that can follow. Being able to understand the limitations of our datasets properly and to explore them qualitatively in an ad-hoc way is a necessary first step to understanding the behavior, the harmful biases and the failure modes of the artifacts built on them. So understanding the training data is a critical step when releasing and auditing large language models.

- Origin and audience
  - open-source tool for quick indexing and deployment of shareable search engines
  - wider audience: IR students, Digital Humanists, Shared Tasks organizers, digital investigative journalists; ad hoc search engines; Section 4
- What it does
  - index text collections, deploy as interactive search apps, editable in browser, shareable with stakeholders
  - "standing on the shoulders" of open-source libraries: Castorini (cite), Hugging Face (cite), Python
  - interoperability -> quick indexing, free deployment of search interfaces; less overhead operationalizing data governance; data analysis over data engineering
  - modular design: data loading (Section 3.1), preprocessing (Section 3.2), dense and sparse indexing (Sections 3.3), creation (Section 3.1), free hosting of graphical search interfaces (Section 3.5)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The commoditization of data has transformed data-driven computer science in general, and machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) in particular. The race to train larger and larger language models depends so much on having access to huge amounts of text that the datasets have become "too big to document", as one paper claims, both technically and methodologically. In practice this often leads to training first and asking questions later, which is an example of a convenience experiment, meaning a research approach that depends on the availability of a resource and on how easy a method is rather than on whether it suits the problem. In this sense, some authors believe it is important to distinguish between the availability of data and its appropriateness, especially because of the misconception that web data represents all human experience and is immune to the digital divide, which keeps getting wider. They suggest that the divide exists and also limits the representativeness of the web, and this in turn reinforces the biases of the artifacts that use it.

Since large datasets can't be easily audited, researchers are incentivized to release models trained on data they don't really understand, and this leads to model behaviors that are hard to study, predict or trace. This is especially a problem because of the real-world harms that can follow. Being able to understand the limitations of our datasets properly and to explore them qualitatively in an ad-hoc way is a necessary first step to understanding the behavior, the harmful biases and the failure modes of the artifacts built on them. So understanding the training data is a critical step when releasing and auditing large language models.

This is why we first developed Spacerini, as an open-source tool for quickly indexing and deploying shareable search engines. But since then we have realized it could also be useful for a wider audience that wants to make their text artifacts searchable. This includes IR students, Digital Humanists, Shared Tasks organizers and digital investigative journalists, who all want to quickly deploy ad hoc search engines for their research. We describe these use cases in more detail in Section 4.

Spacerini makes the process of auditing large datasets easier by letting users index their text collections with little effort and deploy them as interactive search applications, which can be easily edited in the browser and shared with all stakeholders. It does this by "standing on the shoulders" of battle-tested open-source libraries from the Castorini, Hugging Face and Python ecosystems. It also improves the interoperability between them, so that search interfaces can be indexed quickly and deployed for free in an easy-to-use package. This reduces the overhead usually involved in operationalizing data governance frameworks and lets stakeholders focus on data analysis instead of data engineering. This is possible because of its modular design, which enables data loading (Section 3.1), preprocessing (Section 3.2), dense and sparse indexing (Sections 3.3), and the creation (Section 3.1) and free hosting of graphical search interfaces (Section 3.5) for text datasets.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The commoditization of data has transformed data-driven computer science in general [1] and machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) in particular [2]. The race to train ever-larger language models depends so much on access to immense amounts of text [3] that the datasets have become, as [4] claims, both technically [4] and methodologically [5] "too big to document". In practice, this often leads to an approach of training first and asking questions later [6], which is again an example of a convenience experiment [7]: a research approach that depends on the availability of a resource and the ease of a method rather than its suitability to the problem at hand. In this sense, [8] believe it is important to distinguish between the availability of data and its appropriateness, especially in light of the misconception that web data represents all human experience and is immune to the ever-widening digital divide [9]. They suggest that the divide not only exists, but limits the representativeness of the web, which in turn reinforces the biases of the artifacts that use it [4].

Being unable to easily audit large datasets incentivizes researchers to release models trained on data they do not truly understand [2], leading to model behaviors that are hard to study, predict or trace [2,10,11]. This is especially problematic given the potential real-world harms that ensue [12,13,14,15]. Being able to properly understand the limitations of our datasets and to qualitatively explore them in an ad-hoc fashion is a necessary first step toward understanding the behavior, harmful biases and failure modes of the artifacts built upon them. Understanding the training data is therefore a critical step in releasing and auditing large language models [16].

It is from this vantage point that we initially developed Spacerini as an open-source tool for the quick indexing and deployment of shareable search engines, but we have since come to realize its potential usefulness for an even wider audience interested in making their text artifacts searchable. This includes IR students, Digital Humanists, Shared Tasks organizers, and digital investigative journalists, all of whom seek to quickly deploy ad hoc search engines for their research. We cover these use cases in more detail in Section 4.

Spacerini helps streamline the process of auditing large datasets by allowing users to effortlessly index their text collections and deploy them as interactive search applications that can be easily edited in the browser and shared with all stakeholders. It achieves this by "standing on the shoulders" of battle-tested open-source libraries from the Castorini [17], Hugging Face [18,19] and Python ecosystems. It also enhances the interoperability between them to enable quick indexing and free deployment of search interfaces in an easy-to-use package, which reduces the overhead typically involved in operationalizing data governance frameworks and allows stakeholders to focus on data analysis rather than data engineering. This is achieved through its modular design, which enables data loading (Section 3.1), preprocessing (Section 3.2), dense and sparse indexing (Sections 3.3), as well as the creation (Section 3.1) and free hosting of graphical search interfaces (Section 3.5) for text datasets.
